doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Moving to America and admiring American players
summary: He stayed in Italy until marrying at 33, then moved to the US to learn from exceptional musicians; in Milan they revered American jazz players such as Tommy Flanagan and Barry Harris.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: All right. So just to wrap up. Do you think you’ll spend the rest of your life in America?

Well it’s hard to say. Because I’ll tell you something very funny. When I was still living with my parents, you know, I used to say — you know I stayed with my parents until I got married. I have nothing against this. You know here in America most of the kids, when they go to college they leave their families. I stayed with my parents until age 33, before getting married. Then I got married and I moved to the United States. But before meeting the one beautiful girl that I married, you know I was sure one hundred percent that I would have never left Italy. I loved my country and I felt everything was fine. I didn’t have no problem. But then, coming to the United States I came across some exceptional musicians that I felt very much that I could learn from them. And I needed to learn from them. I wanted to evolve. And so everything happened very quickly. One thing led to another. And when you are in the moment you’re not sure exactly where is the path going, but then when you look back you are amazed. And so I’m very happy to be here. I’m very happy to be working and to play with wonderful jazz musicians. You know I’m going to say one more thing to conclude this interview that might give you an idea. You see when I was in Milan, we felt, I mean myself and some of my colleagues in Milan, we felt that the way some American musicians played jazz was really special. And somehow we felt that that was the right way. In other words in some of these American

musicians there was that kind of authenticity in the music, of course, it is the music of their own country you know. And so every time we knew that there was a famous American jazz players that would tour Italy and come to Milan or close by Milan we would go hear him. So we went to hear Tommy Flanagan in Milan. We went to hear Kenny Barron once near Modena. I went once all the way to Switzerland in Bern, almost 400 km from my own town to hear again the Tommy Flanagan Trio, and then Barry Harris came you know, almost every year. Still going there to Italy. So every time we heard one of these musicians playing we heard that there was something way superior. And so what happened was that when we would play gigs, with my Milanase colleagues, and one of us would play very well, the most beautiful compliment that we could tell each other was, “tonight you sounded like an American.” You know? So this has got nothing to do with the politics. It’s just the fact. Because we felt that the jazz of Coleman Hawkins, the American tradition, was the tradition to follow, the authentic tradition. And I don’t want to offend no one. Because today, now twenty years went by and of course the music spread even more and there are some young musicians from all over the world that they play fantastic. But back then, twenty years ago, that’s what we felt. We had this great admiration for the great American players. And we wanted to sound like them.
